case_name: Global Entertainment Inc. (Global Events) c. Goldfarb
text:
Global Entertainment Inc. (Global Events) c.
Goldfarb

2011 QCCS
2324

JS1319

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

N°:

500-17-048765-096

DATE:

May 5, 2011

______________________________________________________________________

PRESIDING:

THE HONOURABLE

MARK SCHRAGER, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

GLOBAL ENTERTAINMENT INC, doing business as
Global Events

Plaintiff/
Cross-Defendant

v.

MICHAEL GOLDFARB

Defendant/Cross-Plaintiff

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

Plaintiff, Global Entertainment Inc ("Global"), claims damages
from its former employee, the Defendant Michael Goldfarb ("Goldfarb")
[1]

based on an employment contract Exhibit P-1, which contains non-compete,
non-solicitation and liquidated damages clauses. Goldfarb denies liability,
claiming he was wrongfully dismissed from his employment and as such is not
bound by the aforementioned clauses. Moreover, Goldfarb claims in his
Cross-Demand, damages in his own right stemming from the alleged wrongful
dismissal, which he has characterized as a constructive dismissal.

FACTS:

[
2
]

Global is the company of its founder Mr. Oliver Friedman
("Friedman") who started it in 1994 when he worked as a disc jockey
("DJ") at private parties. He has grown the company to render all
manner of entertainment services for private parties such as weddings, bar and
bat mitzvahs, graduations and fashion shows. The services rendered include
providing DJs, masters of ceremonies ("MCs"), dancers and other
animators as well as renting lighting and sound equipment. Global will service
as many as 400 such events annually. Events can cost as much as $200,000.
According to Friedman's testimony and as evidenced by much of the proof, the
bulk of Global's clientele are members of the Montreal Jewish community
resident in the western part of the Island of Montreal. The market does however
go beyond this as Global has serviced events in Brossard, LaSalle, the
Laurentians, Eastern Townships and to a lesser extent in Toronto, Detroit and
Ottawa. Exhibit P-44 is a list of places where Global has performed.

[
3
]

Much of the marketing of Global is accomplished by word-of-mouth, i.e.
by people who have seen the product at an event and are positively impressed.
They will subsequently contact Global and seek to reserve its services for an
event that they are planning. Written contracts are not signed although Global
has an internal booking form (for example see Exhibit P-45). Global also places
advertisements in local media and renders services (often without charge or at
reduced rates) at events which will provide exposure to large groups of potential
clients (for example at functions at some of the local private Jewish schools).

[
4
]

At the beginning of 2009, other than Friedman, there were only two
full-time employees of Global. The other "staff" are not salaried
employees but independent contractors. However, some, such as DJs will work
exclusively for Global. Others, such as suppliers of equipment, will supply
anybody in the industry including competitors of Global.

[
5
]

Goldfarb was a salaried employee of Global up until the end of December
2008. He first met Friedman in 1998. Goldfarb was a popular DJ when he was
hired by Friedman and his popularity grew. Customers would specifically request
that he be the DJ at the event for which they engaged Global. Goldfarb worked
for Global from 1998 to 2001 when he left for a competitor and at which time a
good deal of business followed him either because it was solicited or
spontaneously. In 2004, Friedman encountered Goldfarb who was not working and
it was agreed by the two that Goldfarb would return to work for Global as an
independent contractor providing DJ, MC and sales representative services.
Because he was wary of the loss of business encountered when Goldfarb left
Global in 2001, Friedman sought legal advice which led to the drafting and the
signature by Goldfarb of Exhibit P-16: "Service Confidentiality,
Non-Competition and Non-Solicitation Agreement" which contains a
restrictive covenant.

[
6
]

In 2004, Goldfarb said he wanted to cease being an independent
contractor and become an employee of Global. Friedman agreed and Exhibit P-1
was signed on August 15, 2007. Paragraphs 3 and 4 of Exhibit P-1 read as
follows:

"3.
Non-Competition

During the term of the
Employee's
employment, or
any extension or renewal thereof, and for a period of six (6) months thereafter,
the Employee shall not, directly or indirectly, alone or as a partner,
consultant, officer, director, employee, independent contractor to or
shareholder of any company or business organization engage, whether directly or
indirectly, in any of the activities more fully described in Schedule
"A" hereof. The foregoing restriction shall apply throughout the
geographic area outlined in Schedule "B" attached hereto. The
Employee must inform Global of any and all solicitation offers from any of
Global's
competitors
.

4.
Non-Solicitation of employee, customers
and suppliers

During the term of the present Agreement, or renewal
thereof, and for a period of twelve (12) months thereafter, the Employee shall
not, directly or indirectly, alone or as a partner, consultant, officer,
director, employee, independent contactor to or shareholder of any company or
business organization, solicit, interfere with or endeavor to entice away any
employee, customer or supplier of GLOBAL or any prospective employee, supplier
or customer of GLOBAL who is such at the time of termination of the Employee's
employment. For the purpose of this section "prospective" shall mean
one with whom substantive discussions have taken place and whose change of
status to employee, customer or supplier, respectively, is imminent".

[
7
]

It is also in evidence that in the first year of his employment,
Goldfarb earned between $40,000 and $45,000 per year. By the end of 2008 he was
earning $55,000 a year. Moreover, it is also in evidence that between 19 and
25% of his total compensation was represented by the salaried portion of his
remuneration, namely $225 per week. The balance was commissions and DJ fees.

[
8
]

According to Friedman, in consideration of the $225 salary per week,
Goldfarb was supposed to perform marketing services (although this is not
mentioned in Exhibit P-1) as well as scheduling staff (i.e. making sure that
events were properly staffed with the appropriate people such as DJs, dancers,
MCs, etc.) as well as office work which included, according to Friedman the
"branding of the Company". The contract Exhibit P-1 did not provide
for, nor did Friedman indicate to Goldfarb the number of hours that should be
physically spent in the office premises of Global. Goldfarb was not given by
Friedman any specific instructions on how to do his job. Specifically, Friedman
did not instruct Goldfarb on the number of staff meetings which should be held
in the course of any calendar year. As will be seen later, one of the
complaints of Friedman leading to the termination of the employment of Goldfarb
was the latter’s failure to convene staff meetings.

[
9
]

Since 2004, Goldfarb always received the bonuses provided for in Exhibit
P-1 by attaining the performance targets reflected therein. However, he never
attracted sufficient new corporate business to attain the commission stipulated
in Exhibit P-1 with regard thereto. According to Friedman no new corporate
business was brought in by Goldfarb. However, according to Goldfarb some
$20,000 to $30,000 of new corporate business was brought in by him. In any
event this was not enough to trigger the 10% commission on new corporate
accounts stipulated in schedule B to Exhibit P-1. According to Goldfarb, this
clause in the contract was not so much a requirement of the level of services
he was obliged to achieve but rather a means of increasing his earnings.
Goldfarb explained that it was difficult to attract corporate business since
the image of Global in the community as reflected on its website labeled it an
entertainment company geared to adolescents. This made it difficult to break
into the corporate market. Goldfarb was by all accounts a good DJ and
apparently, good at attracting private party business and was competent at
organizing and staffing them.

[
10
]

Given that Exhibit P-1 ran from September to September, Friedman and
Goldfarb met to renegotiate the remuneration terms of Exhibit P-1 during the
summer of 2008. Despite this reference to a term, Exhibit P-1 was treated by
both parties as a contract of employment of indefinite term. When the parties
failed to agree on the terms and conditions by September 1, 2008 they both
continued to treat the employment as ongoing.

[
11
]

The negotiations during the summer of 2008 were marked by criticism from
Friedman of the performance of Goldfarb. Friedman felt that Goldfarb convened
an insufficient number of staff meetings (although historically there have only
been a maximum of two or three per year). Friedman also complained that
Goldfarb was not present in the office for a sufficient number of hours in any
given week.

[
12
]

Goldfarb testified that no complaints about his services were received
at this time but is contradicted by the e-mail letter, Exhibit P-17 dated
August 12, 2008 sent by Friedman to Goldfarb complaining about his services. Goldfarb
described this as Friedman's negotiating tactics.

[
13
]

By September 2008, no new agreement on remuneration had been agreed to
by Friedman and Goldfarb although the $225 per week for office work was
increased to $250 per week as an interim measure.

[
14
]

Both parties seem to agree that Goldfarb was less motivated after
September 1, 2008 following the failed negotiation either because, according to
Friedman, after such failed negotiation Goldfarb was preparing an exit strategy
from Global or, according to the evidence of Goldfarb, he was being excluded by
Friedman. The example of not being given a key or door access code to the new
premises to which Global moved is given by Goldfarb as the proof of such
exclusion. It is obvious that the failure to come to terms on a remuneration
package going forward brought tension to the parties' relationship by September
2008. Friedman wanted to retain Goldfarb for his DJ and party organizing
skills. Goldfarb was looking for a bigger role in Global and potentially a
partnership or equity interest.

[
15
]

The parties discussed a furniture rental venture which might translate
into equity participation for Goldfarb but these discussions did not result in
any agreement.

[
16
]

Since no new remuneration agreement had been achieved by late 2008, Friedman
invited Goldfarb to put his contract demands in writing. Consequently Goldfarb
wrote by e-mail to Friedman on December 22, 2008. Exhibit P-3 reads in part as
follows:

"
Base Salary

$500/wk

$350/wk (Research, Marketing,
Promotion-Toronto/Montreal)

$150/wk (Scheduling, staff Management)

Guaranteed to be in the office for a minimum of 25
hrs/wk.

[…]

Like I mentioned to you during our meeting today, I
don’t want these negotiations to drag on like last time. As much as it is my
intention to get a deal done. I don’t think I’d be able to handle that kind of
stress again! The season has come to an end now is the perfect time to focus on
this so that we both know where we stand this upcoming year. Therefore, I have
set my own personal deadline of Dec. 26
th
, 2008- 12PM to
either move forward or walk away.

Thanks & I look forward to hearing back from you
soon.

Michael"

[
17
]

Friedman did not agree with the remuneration demands in Exhibit P-3.
Goldfarb's deadline for reply was December 26, 2008. Friedman replied in writing
on December 29, 2008 (Exhibit P-4), cited below.

[
18
]

Goldfarb testified that he was at the office on December 29, 2008 and
when he saw Friedman, he was invited to "check your e-mails". He read
Exhibit P-4 and in his words, felt that he had been dismissed, so he took his
computer and left the Global premises.

[
19
]

Exhibit P-4 reads in part as follows:

"Mike

I’ve reviewed your proposal but at this point, I
don’t intend to address each clause individually. Instead, I will outline what
I perceive to have been the situation for the last several months.

Several years ago, you were given 3 areas of
responsibility: office work including staff hiring and scheduling as well as
marketing and promotion of Global for which you were paid a weekly salary,
DJing for which you were paid a set fee and handling events for which you were
paid a commission.

Over the last year, we have frequently discussed your
lack of performance, particularly in terms of marketing Global and your failure
to bring in new business. As you put it, for the last 6 months, you have been
“missing in action”. Over the last month alone, you have not been in the office
more than 10 hours.

[…]

Considering the above, I am not prepared to agree to
your proposal. I have always tried to be reasonable and I honestly believe that
if you are prepared to respect your obligations, we can come to a mutually
satisfactory arrangement. However, by your own admission, you have not been
doing the work for which you were being paid a weekly salary. I have no choice
but to consider that you have renounced this aspect of your employment
pertaining to the office and marketing work for which you were paid a weekly
salary. Accordingly, until such time as we reach a mutually satisfactory
arrangement, you will be relieved from all office and marketing tasks. I will
continue to pay you your current rate for DJing and you will of course continue
to receive commission on events that you handle.

I am hopeful that we can come to a mutually
satisfactory arrangement because I honestly believe that we both have a lot to
gain from it.

Oliver Friedman

Global Events Inc;"

[
20
]

Goldfarb replied on January 7 (Exhibit P-5) in part as follows:

"Olivier,

Thank you for your email.

What I gather from it was the following:

You have officially decided to turn down the most
recent compensation package that I proposed.

You have relieved me of my duties pertaining to
office work (recruiting, managing and training the entertainment staff),
including the marketing and promotion of Global Events and have elected to cease
payment of my salary (hence the reason I took my computer from the office.)

In this email you have also taken the liberty to
clearly document various aspects of my work at Global over the past several
months. I feel it is only fair that I in turn give my perspective on why our
working relationship has ultimately hit rock bottom:

[…]

Going forward, I’m still worn down from the last
negotiations we went through. Therefore, I don’t have energy to sustain yet
another long and stressful negotiation process with you. We haven’t been
agreeing on much lately so, let’s agree to disagree and move on. I have my
future to worry about now. As you know, I have taken on a lot of expenses these
last couple of years. I have to take a look at my options and figure out a way
to survive! In the meantime, we were both still bound by the agreement of 2007,
until Dec. 29, 2008 when you decided to effectively breach our contact by
ceasing payment of my salary and relieving me of various duties.

Michael Goldfarb"

[
21
]

On January 12, 2009, Global acting through Friedman wrote to Goldfarb
(Exhibit P-6) referring to his "resignation from Global" even though
Exhibit P-5 explicitly states that Goldfarb is being "relieved from his
office duties" at Global. Moreover, Exhibit P-5 states clearly that
Friedman (i.e. Global) will not pay the office portion of Goldfarb's
remuneration although he was still prepared to pay for Goldfarb to handle DJ
and other client services.

[
22
]

Shortly after Goldfarb left the premises on December 29, 2008, he no
longer had access to his Global e-mail account or obviously to the telephone.

[
23
]

By January 29, 2009, Global sent the first of several formal demand
letters to Goldfarb reminding him of the various restrictive covenants in
Exhibit P-1.

[
24
]

Goldfarb's demand letter claiming wrongful constructive dismissal was
sent on March 27, 2009 (Exhibit D-5).

[
25
]

Goldfarb subsequent to his departure from Global was in contact with a
Mrs. Pat Stein who had dealt with Goldfarb to book Global services. Goldfarb
testified that he did not solicit Mrs. Stein nor any other person who had
booked the services of Global. Goldfarb testified that in all instances these
people learned from other sources, including Global of his departure from
Global and contacted Goldfarb via his cell phone number which they were all in
possession of. It was his usual course of business to give customers his cell
phone number.

[
26
]

Goldfarb testified (and this is confirmed by Friedman) that he called
Friedman and they agreed to co-operate whereby Global would conduct the
"Pat Stein event" but Goldfarb would provide the DJ services and
Global would pay him for such services. Despite this agreement, Friedman did
not pay Goldfarb for the DJ services because as he testified he knew that he
would be suing Mr. Goldfarb and decided to set-off such amount against the
amounts he considered that Mr. Goldfarb owed to Global. He did not share this
intention with Mr. Goldfarb at the time.

[
27
]

Despite the allegations, Friedman testified that he was not aware that
these people would have been solicited. Rather he is only aware that they had
booked the services of Global and ultimately after the departure of Goldfarb
had their event conducted by Goldfarb in his new business after January 1,
2009. Some of them forfeited deposits, which Global retained. In order to
confirm that he did not solicit such people Mr. Goldfarb requested the
signature of a form letter to such effect (Exhibit D-4 en liasse).

[
28
]

Goldfarb testified that following legal advice he received at the time
he understood that because he had been dismissed he was not bound by the
non-compete covenant. He quickly set up a Facebook page and commenced operating
under the firm name of "Fresh Entertainment".

[
29
]

Evidence was adduced by Plaintiff to the extent that Goldfarb had
contacted or solicited various suppliers of Global. With the possible exception
of certain DJs, the suppliers were not exclusive to Global.

ISSUES:

[
30
]

Did Defendant resign as an employee of Global Entertainment Inc. or was
he dismissed (i.e. the victim of a constructive dismissal)?

[
31
]

If Defendant was dismissed, was he dismissed for a "serious
reason" within the meaning of Article 2095 of the
Quebec Civil Code

("
C.C.Q."
), i.e. what the case law traditionally calls
"just and sufficient cause"?

[
32
]

In the event that Defendant resigned or was dismissed for serious
reason, are the non-compete and non-solicitation clauses binding on Defendant
within the meaning of Article 2089
C.C.Q.
?

[
33
]

If Defendant is bound by the non-compete and non-solicitation clauses
should the liquidated damages clause in Exhibit P-1 apply as written or be
reduced?

[
34
]

If Defendant was not dismissed for a serious reason, what indemnity must
he be paid by Plaintiff?

[
35
]

Aside from the obligations under the non-compete or non-solicitation
clauses, is Defendant otherwise obliged to pay damages to Plaintiff for passing
off or contravening his duty of loyalty to his employer?

DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS:

[
36
]

Goldfarb and Friedman negotiated new financial terms for Exhibit P-1
throughout the summer of 2008 without reaching an agreement. To the extent that
Exhibit P-1 was a contract of employment of fixed term then it would become a
contract of indeterminate term once Goldfarb continued to work for five days
after September 1, 2008 (Article 2090 C.C.Q.). At some point in September or
early October Goldfarb's base weekly salary for office work was increased from
$225 to $250. The parties were very busy throughout the autumn such that the
negotiations did not resume until the end of December when Friedman invited
Goldfarb to commit his remuneration wishes to writing and so the e-mail,
Exhibit P-3 was sent by Goldfarb to Friedman on December 22, 2008.

[
37
]

In Exhibit P-3, Goldfarb set a deadline of December 26 "to either
move forward or walk away". Despite the absence of reply from Friedman,
Goldfarb attended at the office of Global on December 29, 2008 which Defendant
submits is proof that he had not resigned at that time. While at the office he
received Friedman's reply by e-mail. Exhibit P-4 rejects Goldfarb's proposal
Exhibit P-3 outlining that Goldfarb had not been carrying out the office work
for which he was receiving a weekly fixed salary and Exhibit P-4 goes on to say
that:

"
I have no choice but to consider that you have
renounced this aspect of your employment pertaining to the office and marketing
work for which you were paid a weekly salary. Accordingly, until such time as
we reach a mutually satisfactory arrangement, you will be relieved from all
office and marketing tasks. I will continue to pay you your current rate for
djing and you will of course continue to receive commission on events that you
handle"
.

The office portion of the
remuneration of Goldfarb constituted between 19.5 and 23% of Goldfarb's total
annual remuneration of $50,000 to $60,000. In these circumstances
"relieving" Goldfarb of that position alone would be sufficient in
the eyes of a reasonable person to characterize this change in the conditions
of employment as substantial. Moreover as pleaded by Defendant the loss of face
and the demotion to being a mere DJ and sales representative as opposed to the
person who is hiring and managing all the other DJs was a substantial change to
the essential terms of the contract of employment. The subsequent self-serving
characterization of events by Friedman and his attorney in the correspondence
(Exhibits P-6 and P-8) as a resignation does not change this reality.

[
38
]

Plaintiff pleads that Goldfarb received one written notice of
dissatisfaction about his failure to book corporate business (Exhibit P-17) and
several verbal critiques about insufficient number of staff meetings and
attendance of Goldfarb in the office premises of Global. The proof is vague at
best on what was required of Goldfarb for the number of staff meetings and
hours present at the Global office (see pre-trial examination of Friedman pages
32, 33). Moreover, the proof is absent as to direction by the employer
(pre-trial examination of Friedman pages 32, 33, 35, 38) and vague as to
reprimand (pre-trial examination of Friedman page 52). There were certainly no
written reprimands (pre-trial examination of Friedman pages 31, 32 and 39). The
verbal reprimands seem more like negotiating positions than reprimands. There
was never any warning that failure to call a minimum number of staff meetings
or be present in the office premises for a minimum number of hours per week
would lead to being "relieved of the office portion of Goldfarb's
employment". To the contrary, his salary was increased for these services
in the autumn of 2008. Moreover, Global was apparently pleased with all of the other
services (sales, DJ, staffing of parties) that Goldfarb provided under the
auspices of the employment agreement, Exhibit P-1. Consequently, it appears
that the dismissal was not for serious reason and required sufficient notice to
be given by the employer (Global) to the employee Goldfarb.

[
39
]

Farber
vs.
Royal Trust Company
[2]
is the leading
case on constructive dismissal. Specifically, the Supreme Court of Canada
underlined at paragraph 39 of its judgment that the elimination of a fixed
portion of an employee's remuneration package to leave only the commission
portion is "extremely detrimental to the (employee's) financial
security".

[
40
]

Therefore, the substantial unilateral change by the Plaintiff employer
of the employment agreement, Exhibit P-1 and Defendant employee's refusal of
such change and departure constitute the termination of the employment of
Goldfarb by way of constructive dismissal within the eyes of the law.

[
41
]

Given the Court's conclusion that Goldfarb was dismissed without serious
reason, Article 2095
C.C.Q.
prohibits Global from availing itself of the
non-compete clause. Because the non-compete clause is inapplicable it is not
necessary to analyze its validity as to the reasonableness of its ambit within
the meaning of Article 2089
C.C.Q
.

[
42
]

Does the same reasoning apply to the non-solicitation clause contained
in Exhibit P-1? In
Robitaille
et Multi-Options Nursing Inc

vs
Gestion L. Jalbert
et al
[3]
the Court of
Appeal approved the writings of Mme. Justice Bich, J.C.A. (then Professor Bich)
[4]
in holding that
non-solicitation clauses should be treated for legal purposes as non-compete
clauses. Accordingly, Plaintiff may not avail itself of the non-solicitation
clause. In any event, the evidence of actual solicitation was weak. Friedman
testified that he had no direct knowledge of any customers being solicited.
Goldfarb said that customers contacted him upon learning of his departure from
Global (rather than vice versa) and this was confirmed by the uncontradicted
testimony of at least five such customers (Eisenberg, Moskovitz, Sevy, Maman
and Mizrahi). On the balance of probabilities there does not appear to have
been solicitation of Global customers by Goldfarb.

[
43
]

Plaintiff points to an incident which occurred in October of 2008 where
Goldfarb made arrangements to act as DJ at the Aldo Group holiday party (see
e-mail exchange in Exhibit P-7). Goldfarb arranged to render this service and
be paid personally by the customer. Goldfarb testified at trial that it was
agreed with Global that it was open to him to act as a DJ in a nightclub for
his own account, the rationale being that Global generated most of its profit
from equipment rentals. Since Aldo Group had rented a fully equipped nightclub
for the party, Goldfarb felt that the event fell into this category rather than
that of a corporate party. Friedman did not become aware of the Aldo Group
holiday party until after January 7, 2009 and now submits that this act in
itself constitutes a contravention of the non-compete clause and is grounds for
dismissal. Plaintiff relies on the judgment in
Pro-Quai Inc
vs
Tanguay
[5]

as authority for the proposition that grounds for
dismissal unknown to the employer at the time of dismissal can be relied upon
(in subsequent Court proceedings) to justify the dismissal. In that case, the
past event was relied upon to show intention and that the employee was someone
who would not hesitate to take advantage and use his employment for improper
purposes to the detriment of his employer. As such the Court of Appeal pointed
to the past event to help colour the facts which gave rise to the dismissal as
dishonest and disloyal. Despite his explanation, Goldfarb’s
omission to inform Global colours the incident as a disloyal act though not one
which would give rise to immediate dismissal since it was the first of its kind
by an employee with a good record. At most, a reprimand would have been
justified. However, as a disloyal act Goldfarb should remit (or set-off) the
amount that Global would have earned which would have been $550 of the $750 charged
by Goldfarb to Aldo Group.

[
44
]

Other acts of competition or disloyalty are alleged by Global. Ethos
Design was a contact who might have become a joint venturer or supplier in a
furniture business for Goldfarb and Friedman. Goldfarb spoke to the people with
a view to obtaining employment as their Canadian representative. There is
nothing disloyal
per

se
for an employee to explore or discuss
alternate employment.

[
45
]

The incident involving a Mr. Mike Cohen alleged in the proceedings was
not the subject of any proof at trial.

[
46
]

Given that the employer cannot avail itself of the non-compete or
non-solicitation clauses, the Court need not determine whether in the
circumstances the liquidated damages clause in Exhibit P-1 was reasonable.

[
47
]

The Defendant has claimed six months of severance because he had worked
exclusively for Global since 2004 albeit as an independent contractor until
September 1, 2007 when he became a full-time employee. He was in a managerial
position given his responsibilities to ensure the proper staffing of events
being conducted by Global and the engaging of DJs. He would certainly benefit
from a reasonable notice beyond the statutory minimum under the
Labour
Standards Act
[6]
of two weeks. In
all the circumstances, four months would have been a reasonable notice and so
Defendant should receive salary in lieu thereof. Goldfarb's annual salary
including all commissions had been $ 55,000.00. Thus, four months of salary
would correspond to $18 333. It is common ground between the parties however,
that Defendant had the obligation to mitigate his damages arising from the
wrongful dismissal and indeed, by February 2009 Goldfarb was effectively in
business for himself under the firm name of Fresh Entertainment (Exhibit P-19).
It is also in evidence that during the period January to April 2009, inclusive,
he earned net of expenses $4,560. This should be deducted from the $18,333. The
balance is $13,773.

[
48
]

Defendant also claims unpaid commissions earned as follows: the
so-called "Pat Stein event" where subsequent to Goldfarb's departure
from Global, Friedman specifically agreed to engage Goldfarb and pay him for
his DJ services. An amount of $465 is due. Other events for which Goldfarb
claims commissions on sales booked prior to his departure are the Amzallag Bar
Mitzvah. Based on the evidence an amount of $586 is due to Defendant by
Plaintiff as a commission. With respect to the other event, the Aflalo event,
there is insufficient proof to make any award. With these two amounts there is
$14,824 due to Goldfarb by Global.

[
49
]

After deduction of the amount that should be deducted for the Aldo Group
function there remains $14,274 due to Goldfarb.

[
50
]

Defendant also claimed as Cross-Plaintiff $50,000 damages to his
reputation caused by the sending of the e-mails Exhibit D-6 by Mr. Brandon
Kader, a DJ working for Global. It appears that Mr. Kader worked as an
independent contractor, as was the case with all of the other DJs. Even if this
e-mail, Exhibit P-6 was defamatory (which is doubtful on its face) Mr. Kader
was not an employee of Global and his actions in such regard would not engender
the liability of Global. Moreover, the evidence is that once he learned of
this, Mr. Friedman instructed Kader to stop the e-mails. While there was
mention of other acts of trying to sully Goldfarb's name, the proof was not
specific and though perhaps "close to the line" such matters as
referring to Fresh Entertainment as a company not owning its own equipment and
being unproven and having an uncertain future, did not go beyond tough competition
in the marketplace to reach the point of defamation. There will be no award
with respect to this claim of damage to reputation.

[
51
]

Defendant also claims for "loss of time, stress, trouble and
inconvenience". Again there is no hard proof of these matters. Without in
any way diminishing the time and stress involved in a dispute with a former
employer and present competitor, these are not
per se
actionable
matters. Global did threaten legal proceedings but this was hardly abusive as
it benefited
prima facie
from a non-competition clause even if in the
circumstances this Court concluded that the clause was not applicable.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

]

Plaintiff's action;
